9	
10	# Server Actions — shared machinery
11	
12	Every mutation in Taskflow that a browser can trigger from inside the authenticated
13	dashboard goes through one of the 38 Server Action files under src/actions/. This
14	document is the map of what they have in common before you read the per-domain pages
15	(`actions-auth.md`, `actions-issues.md`, and so on): the `withAction()` wrapper, how the
16	acting principal is resolved, how a Zod parse failure or a thrown domain error turns into
17	the shape a form actually renders, how cache tags get invalidated, and the handful of
18	actions that opt out of all of this because there is no tenant yet to opt into.
19	
20	If you are about to write action number 39, read this file end to end first. Nearly every
21	review comment on a new action in this codebase — "why isn't this going through
22	`withAction()`", "why are you calling `revalidatePath` here" — traces back to something
23	documented on this page.
24	
25	## The `ActionResult` envelope
26	
27	`src/actions/_lib/with-action.ts` and every hand-rolled action agree on one return shape,
28	`ActionResult<T>`, defined in `src/types/api.ts`:
29	
30	```ts
31	type ActionResult<T> =
32	  | { ok: true; data: T; submittedAt: IsoTimestamp }
33	  | { ok: false; error: AppErrorShape; submittedAt: IsoTimestamp };
34	```
35	
36	No action throws across the server/client boundary. A `"use server"` function that threw
37	would surface as an opaque digest in the browser console and nothing else useful; instead,
38	every code path — successful parse, failed parse, thrown domain error — resolves to a
39	value of this shape, and the client form layer branches on `result.ok`. `submittedAt` is
40	not decorative: `useActionState` in React 19 needs some field that changes between two
41	calls to know a *second* submission produced a *new* result even when the payload and the
42	success/failure shape happen to be identical (submit the same invalid form twice in a row,
43	get "the same" error both times — without a changing field the hook would not re-render).
44	The function that stamps it, `stamp()`, lives at the bottom of `with-action.ts` and is
45	private to that module; every action that does not go through `withAction()` — the five
46	described in "Actions with no `Actor` yet" below — sets `submittedAt: new Date().toISOString()`
47	itself at the call site instead, which is the one piece of `withAction()`'s behavior those
48	actions have to reimplement rather than skip. This is DES-223.
49	
50	## `withAction()`: the four responsibilities, in order
51	
52	`withAction<TSchema, TData>(schema, handler, options)` returns the actual exported action
53	function. DES-220 names it the single funnel for validate, authenticate, translate,
54	revalidate, and the implementation performs exactly those four steps in exactly that
55	order:
56	
57	```mermaid
58	sequenceDiagram
59	    participant Form as Client form
60	    participant Action as withAction() closure
61	    participant Schema as Zod schema
62	    participant Actor as getActor / requireActorFor
63	    participant Handler as action handler
64	    participant Service as service layer
65	    participant Cache as revalidateTagged()
66	
67	    Form->>Action: runAction(raw)
68	    Action->>Schema: schema.safeParse(raw)
69	    alt parse fails
70	        Schema-->>Action: ZodError
71	        Action-->>Form: stamp(toActionResult(error))
72	    else parse succeeds
73	        Schema-->>Action: parsed.data
74	        Action->>Actor: resolveActorFor(parsed.data, requireOrg)
75	        alt no session / no active org
76	            Actor-->>Action: throws UnauthorizedActionError
77	            Action-->>Form: stamp(toActionResult(error))
78	        else actor resolved
79	            Actor-->>Action: Actor
80	            Action->>Handler: handler(parsed.data, actor)
81	            alt handler throws
82	                Handler-->>Action: domain error
83	                Action-->>Form: stamp(toActionResult(error))
84	            else handler resolves
85	                Handler->>Service: can() / service call(s)
86	                Service-->>Handler: result
87	                Handler-->>Action: data
88	                Action->>Cache: revalidateTagged(tags, cacheProfile)
89	                Action-->>Form: stamp({ ok: true, data })
90	            end
91	        end
92	    end
93	```
94	
95	1. **Validate.** `schema.safeParse(raw)` runs first, before anything that could touch the
96	   database or the session. A malformed payload never reaches actor resolution, which
97	   matters because actor resolution can itself read `parsed.data` (see below) — an
98	   unvalidated `orgSlug` field is not a safe thing to hand to `getActor()`.
99	2. **Authenticate.** `resolveActorFor()` turns the validated input plus the session cookie
100	   into an `Actor`. This is where `UnauthorizedActionError` gets thrown for a missing or
101	   expired session, before the handler runs at all.
102	3. **Translate errors.** The handler runs inside a `try/catch`; whatever it throws —
103	   `ForbiddenActionError`, `PlanLimitError`, `RateLimitedError`, a service-layer
104	   `PermissionDeniedError`, a Zod error from a nested parse — is caught by the same
105	   `toActionResult()` used for the initial validation failure, so the client never has to
106	   special-case "the error came from parsing" versus "the error came from the handler."
107	4. **Revalidate.** Only after the handler resolves successfully does `withAction()` call
108	   `revalidateTagged(options.revalidate ?? [], options.cacheProfile ?? CACHE_PROFILES.minutes)`.
109	   A thrown error skips this step entirely — there is nothing to revalidate for a mutation
110	   that did not happen.
111	
112	`ActionOptions` is deliberately small: `requireOrg` (default `true`), `revalidate` (a
113	static list of cache tags, distinct from the dynamic ones — `orgTag(id)`, `issueTag(id)` —
114	that the handler itself often calls `revalidateTagged()` with a second time, for the exact
115	row it touched), and `cacheProfile` (the named staleness budget from `CACHE_PROFILES`,
116	required because Next.js 16's `revalidateTag` takes a cache-life profile rather than an
117	implicit default). See `design/caching-and-revalidation.md` for what `CACHE_PROFILES` and
118	tag composition mean in practice (DES-070 through DES-077); this page only covers where
119	the call happens inside the action, not the tag vocabulary itself.
120	
121	## Actor resolution: `requireOrg` and the two input shapes
122	
123	`resolveActorFor(input, fromInput)` inside `with-action.ts` is short but easy to misread on
124	a first pass. When `options.requireOrg` is not explicitly `false` (the default is `true`),
125	it inspects the *already-parsed* input for an `orgSlug` or `orgId` field:
126	
127	- If `orgSlug` is present, it calls `getActor(orgSlug)`, the same helper a Server Component
128	  under `[orgSlug]/` uses.
129	- Else if `orgId` is present, it calls `requireActorFor(orgId as OrgId)`.
130	- Otherwise — or when `requireOrg` is `false` — it falls back to
131	  `getSessionPrincipal()` and resolves the actor against the session's `activeOrgId`,
132	  throwing `UnauthorizedActionError` if there is no session or no active org.
133	
134	This is DES-221: **actor resolution prefers the payload's own org identity over the
135	session default.** The reason is concrete, not stylistic. `changePlanAction` and
136	`updateOrganizationAction` both carry an `orgId` field in their schema — the org being
137	billed or renamed is named explicitly by the form, and if a user has two browser tabs open
138	on two different organizations, the session's "active" org (whichever tab switched last)
139	must not silently override which org the submitted form actually intended to mutate. Only
140	`updateProfileAction` sets `requireOrg: false`: a profile is a `User` row, not a tenant row,
141	its schema carries no `orgId` or `orgSlug` at all, and the wrapper has nothing to prefer
142	over the session default because there is nothing to prefer it to.
143	
144	`getActor()` and `requireActorFor()` themselves — including what a resolved `Actor` looks
145	like and how `assertOrgScope()` fits in — are described in `design/tenant-isolation.md`
146	(DES-032). This page only covers how the action layer decides *which* of the two to call.
147	
148	## Placeholder branded ids for not-yet-existing rows
149	
150	`PermissionResource` (see `design/permission-model.md`, DES-045) is a closed discriminated
151	union keyed by resource kind, and every variant names an id — `issueId`, `projectId`,
152	`commentId`, `memberId`. That is fine when checking "may this actor archive issue X," but
153	awkward when checking "may this actor create an issue in this project," where no issue id
154	exists yet. `src/actions/_lib/permission-resources.ts` exports four placeholder branded
155	ids for exactly this — `PENDING_ISSUE_ID`, `PENDING_PROJECT_ID`, `PENDING_COMMENT_ID`,
156	`PENDING_MEMBER_ID`, each the empty string cast to the branded type — plus
157	`ANONYMOUS_ORG_ID`, used as the rate-limit bucket owner for the handful of actions that run
158	before any org exists (`loginAction`, `requestPasswordResetAction`,
159	`confirmPasswordResetAction`). This is DES-224: reusing the same `PermissionResource` shape
160	for create-time checks works because the ownership escalations inside `can()` compare ids
161	for equality, and an empty string never matches a real ULID, so a create check with a
162	pending id falls straight through to the role matrix — which is exactly the intended
163	behavior, since ownership cannot apply to a row that does not exist yet. You will see
164	`PENDING_PROJECT_ID` passed for `issue:assign`, `issue:update` (via `change-issue-status`
165	and `move-issue`), and `issue:update` in `update-issue.ts` too — all three ask about a
166	specific issue whose `projectId` the action has not fetched, and the role matrix does not
167	consult the project id for those actions, so the placeholder is safe there specifically
168	because the permission check never reads it.
169	
170	## Action-layer error classes
171	
172	`src/actions/_lib/action-errors.ts` declares six error classes that exist *only* in the
173	action layer — services throw their own domain errors (`PermissionDeniedError`,
174	`TenantScopeError`, `FeatureDisabledError`, `AlreadyArchivedError`, `InvalidSlugError`),
175	and repositories throw none at all:
176	
177	| class | `code` | thrown when |
178	|---|---|---|
179	| `UnauthorizedActionError` | `unauthorized` | no session, or the session's active org no longer exists |
180	| `ForbiddenActionError` | `forbidden` | the action-layer `can()` pre-check returned `false` |
181	| `PlanLimitError` | `plan_limit_exceeded` | a count from `@/config/plan-limits` would be exceeded |
182	| `RateLimitedError` | `rate_limited` | `consumeRateLimit()` refused the request |
183	| `FeatureUnavailableError` | `forbidden` | a feature flag gating the whole action evaluates to off |
184	| `ActionNotFoundError` | `not_found` | the row the action addresses is not in the actor's tenant |
185	
186	This is DES-222: these mirror the service-layer domain errors under one closed `ErrorCode`
187	union rather than inventing a second taxonomy the client would have to learn. Notice that
188	`ForbiddenActionError` (thrown by the action's own `can()` pre-check) and
189	`PermissionDeniedError` (thrown by `assertCan()` inside a service) both map to `forbidden`
190	— they exist as separate classes because the action layer already knows the action name at
191	the point of the check and does not need the full `PermissionDecision` object a service's
192	`assertCan()` carries, not because the client needs to tell them apart.
193

# Server Actions — shared machinery

Every mutation in Taskflow that a browser can trigger from inside the authenticated
dashboard goes through one of the 38 Server Action files under src/actions/. This
document is the map of what they have in common before you read the per-domain pages
(`actions-auth.md`, `actions-issues.md`, and so on): the `withAction()` wrapper, how the
acting principal is resolved, how a Zod parse failure or a thrown domain error turns into
the shape a form actually renders, how cache tags get invalidated, and the handful of
actions that opt out of all of this because there is no tenant yet to opt into.

If you are about to write action number 39, read this file end to end first. Nearly every
review comment on a new action in this codebase — "why isn't this going through
`withAction()`", "why are you calling `revalidatePath` here" — traces back to something
documented on this page.

## The `ActionResult` envelope

`src/actions/_lib/with-action.ts` and every hand-rolled action agree on one return shape,
`ActionResult<T>`, defined in `src/types/api.ts`:

```ts
type ActionResult<T> =
  | { ok: true; data: T; submittedAt: IsoTimestamp }
  | { ok: false; error: AppErrorShape; submittedAt: IsoTimestamp };
```

No action throws across the server/client boundary. A `"use server"` function that threw
would surface as an opaque digest in the browser console and nothing else useful; instead,
every code path — successful parse, failed parse, thrown domain error — resolves to a
value of this shape, and the client form layer branches on `result.ok`. `submittedAt` is
not decorative: `useActionState` in React 19 needs some field that changes between two
calls to know a *second* submission produced a *new* result even when the payload and the
success/failure shape happen to be identical (submit the same invalid form twice in a row,
get "the same" error both times — without a changing field the hook would not re-render).
The function that stamps it, `stamp()`, lives at the bottom of `with-action.ts` and is
private to that module; every action that does not go through `withAction()` — the five
described in "Actions with no `Actor` yet" below — sets `submittedAt: new Date().toISOString()`
itself at the call site instead, which is the one piece of `withAction()`'s behavior those
actions have to reimplement rather than skip. This is DES-223.

## `withAction()`: the four responsibilities, in order

`withAction<TSchema, TData>(schema, handler, options)` returns the actual exported action
function. DES-220 names it the single funnel for validate, authenticate, translate,
revalidate, and the implementation performs exactly those four steps in exactly that
order:

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant Form as Client form
    participant Action as withAction() closure
    participant Schema as Zod schema
    participant Actor as getActor / requireActorFor
    participant Handler as action handler
    participant Service as service layer
    participant Cache as revalidateTagged()

    Form->>Action: runAction(raw)
    Action->>Schema: schema.safeParse(raw)
    alt parse fails
        Schema-->>Action: ZodError
        Action-->>Form: stamp(toActionResult(error))
    else parse succeeds
        Schema-->>Action: parsed.data
        Action->>Actor: resolveActorFor(parsed.data, requireOrg)
        alt no session / no active org
            Actor-->>Action: throws UnauthorizedActionError
            Action-->>Form: stamp(toActionResult(error))
        else actor resolved
            Actor-->>Action: Actor
            Action->>Handler: handler(parsed.data, actor)
            alt handler throws
                Handler-->>Action: domain error
                Action-->>Form: stamp(toActionResult(error))
            else handler resolves
                Handler->>Service: can() / service call(s)
                Service-->>Handler: result
                Handler-->>Action: data
                Action->>Cache: revalidateTagged(tags, cacheProfile)
                Action-->>Form: stamp({ ok: true, data })
            end
        end
    end
```

1. **Validate.** `schema.safeParse(raw)` runs first, before anything that could touch the
   database or the session. A malformed payload never reaches actor resolution, which
   matters because actor resolution can itself read `parsed.data` (see below) — an
   unvalidated `orgSlug` field is not a safe thing to hand to `getActor()`.
2. **Authenticate.** `resolveActorFor()` turns the validated input plus the session cookie
   into an `Actor`. This is where `UnauthorizedActionError` gets thrown for a missing or
   expired session, before the handler runs at all.
3. **Translate errors.** The handler runs inside a `try/catch`; whatever it throws —
   `ForbiddenActionError`, `PlanLimitError`, `RateLimitedError`, a service-layer
   `PermissionDeniedError`, a Zod error from a nested parse — is caught by the same
   `toActionResult()` used for the initial validation failure, so the client never has to
   special-case "the error came from parsing" versus "the error came from the handler."
4. **Revalidate.** Only after the handler resolves successfully does `withAction()` call
   `revalidateTagged(options.revalidate ?? [], options.cacheProfile ?? CACHE_PROFILES.minutes)`.
   A thrown error skips this step entirely — there is nothing to revalidate for a mutation
   that did not happen.

`ActionOptions` is deliberately small: `requireOrg` (default `true`), `revalidate` (a
static list of cache tags, distinct from the dynamic ones — `orgTag(id)`, `issueTag(id)` —
that the handler itself often calls `revalidateTagged()` with a second time, for the exact
row it touched), and `cacheProfile` (the named staleness budget from `CACHE_PROFILES`,
required because Next.js 16's `revalidateTag` takes a cache-life profile rather than an
implicit default). See `design/caching-and-revalidation.md` for what `CACHE_PROFILES` and
tag composition mean in practice (DES-070 through DES-077); this page only covers where
the call happens inside the action, not the tag vocabulary itself.

## Actor resolution: `requireOrg` and the two input shapes

`resolveActorFor(input, fromInput)` inside `with-action.ts` is short but easy to misread on
a first pass. When `options.requireOrg` is not explicitly `false` (the default is `true`),
it inspects the *already-parsed* input for an `orgSlug` or `orgId` field:

- If `orgSlug` is present, it calls `getActor(orgSlug)`, the same helper a Server Component
  under `[orgSlug]/` uses.
- Else if `orgId` is present, it calls `requireActorFor(orgId as OrgId)`.
- Otherwise — or when `requireOrg` is `false` — it falls back to
  `getSessionPrincipal()` and resolves the actor against the session's `activeOrgId`,
  throwing `UnauthorizedActionError` if there is no session or no active org.

This is DES-221: **actor resolution prefers the payload's own org identity over the
session default.** The reason is concrete, not stylistic. `changePlanAction` and
`updateOrganizationAction` both carry an `orgId` field in their schema — the org being
billed or renamed is named explicitly by the form, and if a user has two browser tabs open
on two different organizations, the session's "active" org (whichever tab switched last)
must not silently override which org the submitted form actually intended to mutate. Only
`updateProfileAction` sets `requireOrg: false`: a profile is a `User` row, not a tenant row,
its schema carries no `orgId` or `orgSlug` at all, and the wrapper has nothing to prefer
over the session default because there is nothing to prefer it to.

`getActor()` and `requireActorFor()` themselves — including what a resolved `Actor` looks
like and how `assertOrgScope()` fits in — are described in `design/tenant-isolation.md`
(DES-032). This page only covers how the action layer decides *which* of the two to call.

`PermissionResource` (see `design/permission-model.md`, DES-045) is a closed discriminated
